newsitem.title: CHINA: China unveils firms cleared for listing abroad.
newsitem.headline: China unveils firms cleared for listing abroad.

text.p: China unveiled its latest batch of companies cleared to offer shares abroad in a move that could more than double the number of listings outside the country.

It said the plan - which cleared 38 more companies for a foreign listing -- would also help protect the financial interests of Hong Kong, which reverts to Beijing's rule next year and so far has successfully courted most of China's stock offers.
"This will help the regulation and development of China's securities market," said the official China Securities newspaper on Monday.
"It will also help protect and preserve the role of Hong Kong as an international financial centre."
China had cleared a previous batch of 38 companies for foreign stock offers, though only 26 have actually managed to list their shares and 24 of those chose Hong Kong.
Trading on other markets has been sluggish -- though brokers said Tokyo's bourse may lure a few of the latest batch.
Brokers and investment analysts predicted that some of the companies in the latest group of 38 would be snapped up by foreign investors.
Among them were Sanjiu Pharmaceutical Group, a large pharmaceutical firm owned by the People's Liberation Army and based in Guangzhou in southern China.

China World Trade Centre -- which runs the huge commercial complex in Beijing bearing the same name -- is also seen attracting interest as are firms operating roads or investing in China's power sector.
"Companies engaged in basic industry and infrastructure should be attractive," said a broker at J & A Securities in Shenzhen in southern China.
"They should have fairly stable earnings without any nasty surprises," he said.
But some brokers voiced concerns over the prospects of some of China's lumbering state enterprises, and added that interest would be even weaker if the offers were not attractively priced.
"This is a wish list," said Carlton Poon of Worldsec International Ltd in Hong Kong.
"It is not a matter of supply but rather how much the market can absorb."
Other brokers said they were concerned over what appeared to be a political balancing act in the choice of companies, rather than a selection of the best China had to offer.
"This is a balance of regional interests and interests of powerful government-owned organisations," said a Hong Kong broker.
Chinese investment analysts conceded this played a role in the selection but they added there were other factors as well.
"This was an effort to help companies in the (less-developed) northeast and the southwest," said Tao Wei, an investment specialist at People's Insurance Trust and Investment Co.
"But the earnings potential of these companies was also an important factor in the decision," he said.
